extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics
extracted.subtask_short: truth of earth in landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for accurately representing the bare ground, hills, and distant mountains in landscape painting, including geological/structural principles and aerial perspective necessary for truthful depiction. Focuses on form, composition, and the optical effects of distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of earth (faithful representation of bare ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: By truth of earth, we mean the faithful representation of the facts and forms of the bare ground, considered as entirely divested of vegetation, through whatever disguise, or under whatever modification the clothing of the landscape may occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground is to the landscape painter what the naked human body is to the historical. The laws of the organization of the earth are the foundation of all other truths in landscape; ignorance or abandonment of them leads to deformity and falsehood. The artist must study and represent the specific forms of soil, rock, and ground beneath vegetation rather than treating them as generic or decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and obey the laws of the earth's organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of the organization of the earth are distinct and fixed as those of the animal frame... Their results may be arrived at without knowledge of the interior mechanism; but for that very reason ignorance of them is the more disgraceful, and violation of them more unpardonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws are simpler and broader than anatomical laws but equally authoritative. The painter must observe fixed structural principles (how masses support and relate) when composing landscape. Study hill anatomy in situ rather than relying on conventional studio habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hills = action; plains = repose
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains are, to the rest of the body of the earth, what violent muscular action is to the body of man. The plains and the lower hills are the repose and the effortless motion of the frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast between the energetic, expressive forms of mountains and the calm, level surfaces of plains. Convey 'action' in hill forms (sharp ridges, thrusting masses) and 'rest' in plains (level, broad repose). This polarity should inform composition and tonal contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountains spring from beneath the plains (structural support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains are the bones of the earth, their highest peaks are invariably those parts of its anatomy which in the plains lie buried... the mountains must come from under all, and be the support of all; and that everything else must be laid in their arms, heap above heap, the plains being the uppermost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depicting hills as simply 'laid upon' plains. Compose landforms so that higher masses appear to emerge from and be supported by underlying structure; show transitional beds, slopes, and the way lower masses lay upon higher supports. Every minor rock should read as emerging from surrounding soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plains are deposited by water and are level
rubrics_metrics.description: All plains capable of cultivation are deposits from some kind of water... the soil is finally left spread at the exact level of the surface of the former lake, as level as the quiet water itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When painting plains, remember they are often perfectly level deposits (deltas, lake beds). Edges where plains meet steep rock should be abrupt and sharp as lake margins. Treat distant champaigns as broad, water-like surfaces in tone and repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study three-tiered structure: central mountains, interior mountains, foreground
rubrics_metrics.description: The earth may be considered as divided into three great classes of formation... We shall find it convenient... considering first, the formation and character of the highest or central peaks; then the general structure of the lower mountains... and, lastly, the minutiae and most delicate characters of the beds of these hills... and the structure of the common soil which usually forms the greater space of an artist's foreground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize investigation and composition by scale: (1) central/high peaks (character and mass), (2) interior/lower mountains (intermediate structure), (3) foreground soils and details. Each tier has different pictorial treatment and demands different observational emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central peaks: pyramids or wedges with vertical fissures
rubrics_metrics.description: Their summits are almost invariably either pyramids or wedges... These pyramids and wedges split vertically, or nearly so, giving smooth faces of rock, either perpendicular or very steeply inclined... The universal law of fracture is--first, that it is clean and sharp... secondly, that every fissure is steeply inclined, and that a horizontal line, or one approaching to it, is an impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render primary peaks as composed of steep, plank-like beds with vertical fissures and sharp edges; avoid soft, rounded, or horizontal treatment of summit structure. Emphasize clean planar faces and steep fractures in rock masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rock masses arranged like planks or leaves (artichoke/rose analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hence, however the light may fall, these peaks are seen marked with sharp and defined shadows, indicating the square edges of the planks of which they are made up... the peak is often surrounded with groups of lower ridges or peaks, like the leaves of an artichoke or a rose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model mountain masses as assemblies of plates or leaves that form ridges and subsidiary peaks; show intersecting edges and groups falling back from the central mass. Use shadow to indicate the 'plank' edges and the layered nature of the formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant central mountains must be aerial, faint, and lack apparent solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever these mountains are seen over anything like vegetation... they must be at so great a distance from him as to become aerial and faint in all their details... they never can by any possibility have dark or deep shadows, or intense dark relief against a light. Clear they may be, but faint they must be, and their great and prevailing characteristic... is want of apparent solidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not paint distant high mountains with strong local darks or solid modelling. Use pale, opalescent shadows, filmy lights, and an overall aerialized treatment. Avoid 'solid' tones that contradict distance; exemplified by Turner's distant snows (filmy, roseate highlights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of form in extreme distance (no simple outlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicity of form which I have shown to be necessary in the outline, is not less felt in the body of the mass... when chains of such peaks are visible at once, the multiplicity of form is absolutely oceanic... it is physically impossible when these masses are thrown seventy miles back, to have simple outlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At extreme distance, outlines should be broken and jagged—many subordinate ridges and peaks overlap; avoid simplifying distant mountain outlines into single smooth curves. Represent many overlapping vertical films to suggest depth and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant ranges appear as flat vertical films with excessively sharp edges
rubrics_metrics.description: These successive ridges... show themselves in extreme distance merely as vertical shades, with very sharp outlines... You will never, by any chance, perceive in extreme distance, anything like solid form or projection of the hills. Each is a dead, flat, perpendicular film or shade, with a sharp edge darkest at the summit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint distant ridges as flat films (no modelling of solidity), with very keen, decisive outlines—sharper in outline than nearer forms. Use subtle differences of shade between successive films to convey multiple distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharpness of outline, not softened lines, signals extreme distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of extreme distance is always excessive keenness of edge. If you soften your outline, you either put mist between you and the object... or, if you keep an impression of clear air, you bring the object close to the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate distance with fuzzy edges; extreme distance (in clear air) demands very sharp edges. Softening edges implies mist or reduced distance. Choose edge treatment deliberately to communicate whether atmosphere or proximity is at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial transparency and filminess of mass in distant mountains
rubrics_metrics.description: Their lights are pure, roseate, and cloud-like--their shadows transparent, pale, and opalescent, and often indistinguishable from the air around them... the mountain tells only as a flat, sharp-edged film, of which multitudes intersect and overtop one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roseate highlights, opalescent pale shadows, and translucent layers to imply the filmy character of remote snowy peaks. Avoid opaque whites or chalky handling for distant snow; prefer delicate glazing/tonal moderation to convey air between viewer and summit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid classical/old-master anti-patterns: soft, simple, opaque distant mountains
rubrics_metrics.description: Claude's mountains... have soft edges instead of decisive ones, simple forms... and being painted with a crude raw white, having no transparency, nor filminess, nor air in it... They are destitute of energy, of height, of distance, of splendor, and of variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imitate the old-master habit of rendering distant snows as simple, chalky white masses with blunt edges; this produces false distance, lack of magnitude, and a sense of opacity. Use truthful multiplicity of form and aerial color instead. Use Turner's works (e.g., Arona, Alps at Daybreak) as positive examples; use Claude/Stanfield examples as anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: When viewing distance, expect many overlapping lateral chains
rubrics_metrics.description: In all extensive hill ranges, there are five or six lateral chains separated by deep valleys... These successive ridges... wave beyond wave, until the eye is carried back to the faintest and highest forms of the principal chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositionally, render multiple staggered bands of ridge separated by valley-space; indicate each band mainly by its edge and relative faintness. Convey depth by layering many thin tonal steps rather than by modelling individual distant masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe scale-dependent treatments: foreground vs distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout Turner's distances... we have always in them two principal facts forced on our notice; transparency, or filminess of mass, and excessive sharpness of edge... while there is scarcely one decisive edge in the foreground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat foreground with more textural modelling and softer/less decisive contouring appropriate to detail; reserve the sharpest definitive edges and filmy tonal treatments for remote masses. Edge decision and textural detail should vary with depth to communicate scale correctly.
